title: Bones of the Upper Limb
sections: Humerus - Proximal, Shaft, Distal End & Fractures (Q33-Q55)
Radius & Ulna - Borders, Processes, Articulations, Fractures (Q56-Q75)
Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology (Q76-Q100)

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the ossification of the clavicle is correct?
options: It is the first bone in the body to begin ossification.
It ossifies entirely via the endochondral pathway.
It has three primary ossification centers.
It is the last bone in the body to begin ossification.
questions.correctAnswer: A. It is the first bone in the body to begin ossification.
questions.explanation: The clavicle is the first bone to ossify (5th-6th week of fetal life). It ossifies mostly in membrane, but its ends ossify in cartilage.

questions.text: The conoid tubercle is located on which part of the clavicle?
questions.explanation: The conoid tubercle is on the inferior surface of the lateral (acromial) third, serving as an attachment for the conoid ligament.

questions.text: Which muscle originates from the lateral one-third of the anterior border of the clavicle?
questions.explanation: The deltoid originates from the anterior border of the lateral 1/3 of the clavicle.

questions.text: The subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the clavicle provides insertion for which muscle?
questions.explanation: The subclavius muscle inserts into the subclavian groove in the middle third of the clavicle's inferior surface.

questions.text: Fractures of the clavicle most commonly occur at which site?
options: Junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third
questions.correctAnswer: C. Junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third
questions.explanation: The junction of the medial 2/3 (convex) and lateral 1/3 (concave) is the weakest point due to change in curvature and lack of muscle cover.

questions.text: The trapezoid line of the clavicle serves as an attachment for:
questions.explanation: The trapezoid line is for the trapezoid ligament; together with the conoid ligament, they form the coracoclavicular ligament.

questions.text: Which of the following structures passes superior to the clavicle?
questions.explanation: Supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4) descend anterior (superior) to the clavicle to supply skin of the shoulder.

questions.text: The medial end of the clavicle articulates with the manubrium sterni and which costal cartilage?
questions.explanation: The sternal end articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium and the first costal cartilage.

questions.text: In a mid-shaft clavicular fracture, why is the medial fragment displaced superiorly?
questions.explanation: The sternocleidomastoid muscle pulls the medial fragment upwards, while the weight of the arm pulls the lateral fragment down.

questions.text: The nutrient foramen of the clavicle is usually located on the:
options: Inferior surface, medial to the subclavian groove
Inferior surface, lateral to the subclavian groove
questions.correctAnswer: B. Inferior surface, medial to the subclavian groove
questions.explanation: The nutrient foramen usually lies on the inferior surface near the medial end of the subclavian groove, directed laterally.

questions.text: Which ligament prevents the upward displacement of the medial end of the clavicle?
questions.explanation: The costoclavicular ligament anchors the medial end of the clavicle to the first rib.

questions.text: The clavicle is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Though it lacks a medullary cavity and ossifies in membrane, it is traditionally classified as a modified long bone.

questions.text: The lateral end of the clavicle is:
questions.explanation: The lateral (acromial) end is flattened superior-inferiorly to articulate with the acromion.

questions.text: Which muscle is attached to the medial half of the superior surface of the clavicle?
questions.explanation: The clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid attaches to the medial third of the superior surface.

questions.text: An "S" shape is characteristic of the clavicle; which part is convex anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The medial 2/3 is convex anteriorly; the lateral 1/3 is concave anteriorly.

questions.text: The suprascapular notch is converted into a foramen by the:
questions.explanation: The superior transverse scapular ligament bridges the notch; the suprascapular nerve passes under it, and the artery passes over it.

questions.text: Which muscle originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula?
questions.correctAnswer: C. Long head of triceps brachii
questions.explanation: The long head of the triceps brachii originates from the infraglenoid tubercle.

questions.text: The acromion of the scapula articulates with:
options: The lateral end of the clavicle
The medial end of the clavicle
questions.correctAnswer: B. The lateral end of the clavicle
questions.explanation: The acromion articulates with the acromial end of the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint.

questions.text: Which structure attaches to the coracoid process of the scapula?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor inserts on the medial border of the coracoid process.

questions.text: The spinoglenoid notch transmits which of the following?
questions.explanation: The spinoglenoid notch connects the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae, transmitting the suprascapular nerve and vessels.

questions.text: Which muscle is responsible for protracting the scapula and is attached to its medial border?
questions.explanation: Serratus anterior inserts along the whole length of the medial border on the costal surface.

questions.text: The "glenoid labrum" is a fibrocartilaginous ring attached to the:
questions.correctAnswer: C. Margin of the glenoid cavity
questions.explanation: The labrum deepens the glenoid cavity to improve shoulder stability.

questions.text: Which surface of the scapula is marked by three or four ridges for the attachment of the subscapularis muscle?
questions.explanation: These ridges provide attachment for the multipennate subscapularis muscle.

questions.text: The spine of the scapula continues laterally as the:
questions.explanation: The spine of the scapula is a triangular plate that continues laterally as the flattened acromion.

questions.text: Ossification of the scapula typically involves how many centers?
questions.correctAnswer: A. One primary and seven secondary
questions.explanation: Scapula usually has 1 primary (body) and 7 secondary centers (2 for coracoid, 2 for acromion, 1 for medial border, 1 for inferior angle, 1 for glenoid).

questions.text: Winging of the scapula is caused by paralysis of the muscle attached to the:
questions.explanation: Paralysis of Serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve) causes the medial border of the scapula to protrude like a wing.

questions.text: Which muscle is attached to the supraspinous fossa of the scapula?
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus muscle originates from the medial 2/3 of the supraspinous fossa.

questions.text: The lateral border of the scapula is also known as the:
questions.explanation: The lateral border is thick and directed towards the axilla.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles originates from the dorsal surface of the inferior angle of the scapula?
questions.explanation: Teres major originates here; occasionally, a few fibers of latissimus dorsi also attach.

questions.text: The "Safe Zone" for surgical exposure of the scapula often refers to avoid damaging:
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve is at risk during dissection of the supraspinatus or in fractures involving the notch.

questions.text: Type III acromion (hooked) is clinically associated with:
questions.explanation: A 'hooked' acromion reduces the subacromial space, leading to impingement of the rotator cuff.

questions.text: Which ligament forms the "arch" above the head of the humerus to prevent upward dislocation?
questions.explanation: The coracoacromial ligament, coracoid, and acromion form the coracoacromial arch, a 'secondary socket.'

questions.text: Which nerve is most likely to be injured in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels wrap around the surgical neck.

questions.text: The intertubercular (bicipital) groove of the humerus transmits the tendon of:
questions.correctAnswer: B. Long head of biceps brachii
questions.explanation: The tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii (encased in a synovial sheath) lies in this groove.

questions.text: The radial groove (spiral groove) of the humerus is located on the:
questions.explanation: The radial groove (spiral groove) contains the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery on the posterior shaft.

questions.text: Which muscle is attached to the floor of the intertubercular groove?
questions.explanation: Remember 'A Lady between two Majors': Latissimus dorsi (floor) between Pectoralis major (lateral lip) and Teres major (medial lip).

questions.text: The "anatomical neck" of the humerus is:
options: The line separating the head from the tubercles
The constricted part below the tubercles
The attachment site for the deltoid
questions.correctAnswer: A. The line separating the head from the tubercles
questions.explanation: The anatomical neck is the groove separating the head from the greater and lesser tubercles.

questions.text: Supracondylar fractures of the humerus frequently endanger which structure?
questions.explanation: The brachial artery and median nerve are at high risk of injury/compression in supracondylar fractures.

questions.text: The medial epicondyle of the humerus provides origin for the:
questions.correctAnswer: B. Flexor muscles of the forearm
questions.explanation: The medial epicondyle is the 'Common Flexor Origin.'

questions.text: The capitulum of the humerus articulates with the:
questions.explanation: The capitulum (little head) articulates with the superior surface of the radial head.

questions.text: Which nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve (funny bone nerve) sits in a groove on the posterior aspect of the medial epicondyle.

questions.text: The deltoid tuberosity is located on which part of the humeral shaft?
questions.explanation: The deltoid tuberosity is a V-shaped rough area on the lateral aspect of the middle of the humeral shaft.

questions.text: The "carrying angle" of the elbow is primarily formed by the:
options: Downward projection of the medial flange of the trochlea
questions.correctAnswer: B. Downward projection of the medial flange of the trochlea
questions.explanation: The medial edge of the trochlea extends 6mm further distally than the lateral edge, creating an oblique joint line.

questions.text: Ossification of the humeral head usually involves how many secondary centers?
questions.correctAnswer: C. Three (Head, Greater Tuber, Lesser Tuber)
questions.explanation: Secondary centers appear for the head, greater tubercle, and lesser tubercle, which fuse to form one epiphysis.

questions.text: The coronoid fossa is located on the:
options: Posterior aspect of the distal humerus
Anterior aspect of the distal humerus, above the trochlea
Lateral aspect of the proximal humerus
questions.correctAnswer: B. Anterior aspect of the distal humerus, above the trochlea
questions.explanation: The coronoid fossa receives the coronoid process of the ulna during full flexion.

questions.text: Holstein-Lewis fracture is a fracture of the:
options: Distal third of the humeral shaft with radial nerve palsy
questions.correctAnswer: B. Distal third of the humeral shaft with radial nerve palsy
questions.explanation: This refers to a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humerus associated with radial nerve neuropraxia.

questions.text: Which muscle is attached to the lesser tubercle of the humerus?
questions.explanation: Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle that inserts into the lesser tubercle.

questions.text: The "Great Tuberous" of the humerus has three impressions for muscle attachment. Which muscle attaches to the lowest (inferior) impression?
questions.explanation: Superior: Supraspinatus; Middle: Infraspinatus; Inferior: Teres minor.

questions.text: In a fracture of the mid-shaft of the humerus, why does the hand drop?
options: Damage to the radial nerve (paralysis of extensors)
questions.correctAnswer: C. Damage to the radial nerve (paralysis of extensors)
questions.explanation: Radial nerve injury in the spiral groove paralyzes the extensors of the wrist and fingers, causing wrist drop.

questions.text: The nutrient foramen of the humerus is directed:
questions.explanation: Following the rule 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee,' the nutrient foramen of the humerus is directed downwards.

questions.text: Which ligament of the elbow attaches to the lateral epicondyle of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The radial (lateral) collateral ligament originates from the lateral epicondyle.

questions.text: The olecranon fossa receives the olecranon process during:
questions.explanation: The olecranon process enters the fossa on the posterior humerus during elbow extension.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT part of the distal humerus?
questions.explanation: The deltoid tuberosity is located on the shaft (mid-humerus).

questions.text: The common extensor origin is at the:
questions.explanation: The lateral epicondyle is the 'Common Extensor Origin.'

questions.text: Displacement in a proximal humerus fracture at the surgical neck usually results in the proximal fragment being:
questions.correctAnswer: B. Abducted by the rotator cuff
questions.explanation: The proximal fragment is abducted by the supraspinatus/rotator cuff, while the distal fragment is pulled medially/upward by pectoralis major.

questions.text: The radial tuberosity provides insertion for the:
questions.explanation: The biceps brachii tendon inserts into the posterior rough part of the radial tuberosity.

questions.text: The "styloid process" is found on which ends of the radius and ulna?
questions.explanation: Both bones have styloid processes at their distal ends; the radial styloid is more distal than the ulnar styloid.

questions.text: Which bone is the "stabilizing bone" of the forearm and is longer of the two?
questions.explanation: The ulna acts as the stabilizing bone; the radius rotates around it.

questions.text: The trochlear notch of the ulna articulates with the:
questions.explanation: The trochlear notch (semilunar notch) articulates with the trochlea of the humerus.

questions.text: Colles' fracture is a fracture of the:
options: Distal end of the radius with posterior displacement
Distal end of the radius with anterior displacement
questions.correctAnswer: B. Distal end of the radius with posterior displacement
questions.explanation: Fracture of the distal radius (within 2.5cm of the joint) with dorsal (posterior) displacement and angulation.

questions.text: The interosseous membrane is attached to which border of the radius?
questions.explanation: The medial border of the radius is the interosseous border (sharp).

questions.text: Monteggia fracture-dislocation involves:
options: Fracture of the distal radius with dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint
Fracture of the proximal third of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head
Fracture of both radius and ulna
questions.correctAnswer: B. Fracture of the proximal third of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head
questions.explanation: Monteggia: Fracture of the proximal ulna + anterior dislocation of the radial head.

questions.text: The Lister's tubercle is found on the:
options: Distal end of the radius, posterior surface
questions.correctAnswer: B. Distal end of the radius, posterior surface
questions.explanation: Lister's tubercle acts as a pulley for the tendon of the extensor pollicis longus.

questions.text: Which muscle inserts into the olecranon process of the ulna?
questions.explanation: The triceps brachii inserts into the posterior part of the superior surface of the olecranon.

questions.text: The "oblique cord" of the forearm extends from the ulna to the radius just below the:
questions.explanation: The oblique cord is a fibrous band extending from the ulnar tuberosity to the radius just below the radial tuberosity.

questions.text: Which structure articulates with the ulnar notch of the radius?
questions.explanation: The ulnar notch of the radius articulates with the head of the ulna (distal radioulnar joint).

questions.text: A "Smith's fracture" is also known as a:
questions.explanation: Smith's fracture involves anterior (volar) displacement of the distal radial fragment.

questions.text: The supinator crest and supinator fossa are features of the:
questions.explanation: The supinator crest and fossa are on the lateral surface of the upper ulna.

questions.text: Which muscle originates from the anterior surface of the distal quarter of the ulna?
questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus originates from the distal 1/4 of the anterior ulna and inserts into the distal 1/4 of the anterior radius.

questions.text: The "Radial Notch" is a feature of which bone?
questions.explanation: The radial notch is on the lateral side of the coronoid process of the ulna for articulation with the radial head.

questions.text: During pronation and supination, the bone that primarily moves is the:
questions.explanation: In pronation, the radius crosses over the ulna, which remains relatively stationary.

questions.text: The nutrient foramen of the radius is directed:
questions.explanation: The nutrient foramen of the radius is directed upwards (towards the elbow).

questions.text: Galeazzi fracture involves:
options: Fracture of the distal third of the radius with dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint
questions.correctAnswer: A. Fracture of the distal third of the radius with dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint
questions.explanation: Galeazzi: Fracture of the distal radius + dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint.

questions.text: The coronoid process is part of the:
questions.explanation: The coronoid process is the anterior projection of the proximal ulna.

questions.text: Which ligament holds the head of the radius in the radial notch of the ulna?
questions.explanation: The annular ligament encircles the head of the radius and holds it against the ulna.

questions.text: Which carpal bone is the most frequently fractured?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually from a fall on an outstretched hand.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which carpal bone is a sesamoid bone in the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris?
questions.explanation: The pisiform is a sesamoid bone located within the Flexor Carpi Ulnaris tendon.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The "Hook" is a characteristic feature of which carpal bone?
questions.explanation: The hamate has a prominent process on its palmar surface called the hook (hamulus).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which carpal bone is the first to ossify?
questions.explanation: The capitate is the first to ossify (usually in the 1st year).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The most commonly dislocated carpal bone is the:
questions.explanation: The lunate is the most commonly dislocated carpal bone (anteriorly).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which carpal bone articulates with the first metacarpal to form a saddle joint?
questions.explanation: The trapezium articulates with the 1st metacarpal at the thumb base (saddle joint).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The carpal tunnel is formed by the carpal bones and the:
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) converts the carpal groove into a tunnel.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Guyon's canal (ulnar canal) is located between the pisiform and the:
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve and artery pass through Guyon's canal between the pisiform and hamate hook.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The "Boxer's fracture" typically involves the neck of the:
questions.explanation: A Boxer's fracture is a fracture of the neck of the 5th metacarpal (sometimes the 4th).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which carpal bone articulates with the radius?
questions.explanation: The distal radius articulates with the scaphoid and lunate.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: A "Bennett's fracture" is a fracture-dislocation of the base of the:
questions.explanation: Bennett's fracture is an intra-articular fracture at the base of the 1st metacarpal.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: How many phalanges are there in one human hand?
questions.explanation: 3 phalanges for each finger (12) + 2 for the thumb = 14 total.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The largest carpal bone is the:
questions.explanation: The capitate is the largest carpal bone and occupies the center of the carpus.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Avascular necrosis is a common complication of a fracture in the:
questions.correctAnswer: B. Proximal pole of the scaphoid
questions.explanation: Blood supply to the scaphoid enters distally; a proximal pole fracture often cuts off the blood supply.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The tubercle of the scaphoid and the ridge of the trapezium provide attachment for the:
options: Lateral side of the flexor retinaculum
Medial side of the flexor retinaculum
questions.correctAnswer: A. Lateral side of the flexor retinaculum
questions.explanation: These two lateral bony landmarks serve as the lateral attachments for the flexor retinaculum.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which carpal bone is wedge-shaped and located between the scaphoid and triquetrum?
questions.explanation: The lunate (moon-shaped) is located between the scaphoid and triquetrum in the proximal row.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The base of the 3rd metacarpal has a styloid process on its:
questions.explanation: The styloid process of the 3rd metacarpal is on the lateral part of its dorsal base.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which carpal bone is the last to ossify?
questions.explanation: The pisiform is the last to ossify (around age 9-12).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The 1st metacarpal is:
options: The shortest and most mobile metacarpal
questions.correctAnswer: B. The shortest and most mobile metacarpal
questions.explanation: The 1st metacarpal is shorter, thicker, and set at an angle to the others for opposition.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Terrible Triad of the elbow involves a fracture of the coronoid process, a fracture of the radial head, and:
questions.correctAnswer: B. Posterior dislocation of the elbow
questions.explanation: This is a severe elbow injury: Radial head fracture + Coronoid fracture + Posterior dislocation.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which carpal bone articulates with the 2nd metacarpal?
questions.explanation: The trapezoid articulates specifically with the base of the 2nd metacarpal.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The base of a metacarpal bone is its:
questions.explanation: The base is the proximal end; the head is the distal end (knuckle).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Which bone is found in the floor of the "Anatomical Snuffbox"?
questions.explanation: Both the scaphoid (proximally) and trapezium (distally) form the floor of the snuffbox.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: The "dinner fork deformity" is associated with:
questions.explanation: Colles' fracture produces the characteristic dinner fork deformity due to posterior displacement.
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology

questions.text: Ossification of the metacarpals typically involves:
options: One primary center in the shaft
One secondary center in the head (except the 1st)
One secondary center in the base (for the 1st)
questions.explanation: Metacarpals have a primary center in the shaft and one secondary center (head for 2-5, base for 1).
questions.section: Carpal Bones, Metacarpals, Phalanges & Hand Osteology
